prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

“A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands,” my father would say. And he’d prove it, cupping the buzzer instantly while the host with the swatter stared. In the spring our palms peeled like snakes. True Arabs believed watermelon could heal fifty ways. I changed these to fit the occasion. Years before, a girl knocked, wanted to see the Arab. I said we didn’t have one. After that, my father told me who he was, “Shihab”—“shooting star”— a good name, borrowed from the sky. Once I said, “When we die, we give it back?” He said that’s what a true Arab would say. Today the headlines clot in my blood. A little Palestinian dangles a truck on the front page. Homeless fig, this tragedy with a terrible root is too big for us. What flag can we wave? I wave the flag of stone and seed, table mat stitched in blue. I call my father, we talk around the news. It is too much for him, neither of his two languages can reach it. I drive into the country to find sheep, cows, to plead with the air: Who calls anyone civilized? Where can the crying heart graze? What does a true Arab do now?

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Arab, And, True

outputs.L1:
“A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands,” my father would say. And he would prove it, instantly cupping the buzzer while the host stood staring, swatter in hand. In spring, our palms peeled like snakes. True Arabs believed watermelon could heal in fifty ways. I adapted these truths to suit the occasion.

Years before, a girl knocked at our door, asking to see the Arab. I told her we didn’t have one. Afterward, my father told me who he was: “Shihab”—“shooting star”—a good name, borrowed from the sky. Once, I asked, “When we die, do we give it back?” He said that was what a true Arab would say.

Today, the headlines clot in my blood. A little Palestinian dangles a truck on the front page. Homeless fig, this tragedy, with its terrible root, is too vast for us. What flag can we wave? I wave the flag of stone and seed, a table mat stitched in blue.

I call my father, and we talk around the news. It is too much for him; neither of his two languages can reach it. I drive into the country to find sheep and cows, to plead with the air: Who calls anyone civilized? Where can the crying heart graze? What does a true Arab do now?
outputs.L2:
My father used to insist that any genuine Arab could snatch a fly barehanded. Then, while a host stood frozen with a swatter, he would close his palms around the insect in a flash. Each spring, the skin on our hands shed like a snake’s. Real Arabs, he said, knew fifty cures involving watermelon. I adjusted such sayings whenever circumstances required.

Long ago, a girl came to our door asking to meet “the Arab.” I told her no such person lived there. Only afterward did my father explain himself to me: he was Shihab, a name taken from the heavens, meaning “shooting star.” Once I asked whether we return our names when we die. He replied that the question itself was worthy of a true Arab.

Now the news thickens inside my veins. On the newspaper’s front page, a small Palestinian hangs from a truck. Like a fig torn from its home, this catastrophe has roots too dreadful and vast for us to hold. Which banner could possibly represent it? I raise instead a standard made of rock and seed, like a table covering embroidered in blue.

When I phone my father, we circle the headlines without naming them directly. Their weight overwhelms him; neither language he speaks can express what has happened. I drive beyond the city, searching for cattle and sheep, and appeal to the open air: Who has the right to call another person civilized? Where might a grieving heart find pasture? In such a moment, how is a true Arab supposed to act?
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s understanding of Arab identity is shaped first by her father, who expresses his heritage through inherited sayings, folk beliefs, and cultural traditions. For him, Arabness is not merely a matter of ancestry or geography; it is preserved in the language, customs, and stories passed from one generation to the next. Yet as a child, the speaker distances herself from this heritage, perhaps because she does not fully understand its value. This changes when she learns the meaning and significance of her father’s name, “Shihab,” a name that links him—and eventually her—to a wider cultural and symbolic world.

Her father teaches her that being a “true Arab” involves a particular way of thinking. Identity, in his view, is deeply connected to language and to the natural world. Words, names, landscapes, and inherited wisdom all carry meaning, creating a sense of belonging that extends beyond the individual. Arabness therefore becomes not simply an ethnic label but a way of interpreting experience and understanding one’s place in the world.

This understanding becomes more painful and urgent when the speaker encounters news of Palestinian suffering. She is overwhelmed by the violence and experiences the tragedy as both personal and collective. The suffering of others feels inseparable from her own identity, as though it affects not only individual Palestinians but the broader Arab community and its shared history. Faced with such devastation, however, she finds that ordinary language and familiar symbols are inadequate. She cannot fully express the scale of the grief or reconcile cultural pride with the brutality she witnesses.

As a result, the speaker begins to question the meaning of civilization, belonging, and Arab identity itself. She wonders what it means to be a “true Arab” when violence threatens the people, language, land, and traditions that sustain that identity. Her reflections reveal a struggle between inherited cultural meaning and the unbearable realities of the present. Ultimately, Arabness emerges as both a source of connection and a burden of collective grief: an identity rooted in language, memory, and nature, but also profoundly shaped by loss and suffering.
outputs.L4:
I can’t reconstruct the original poem from a summary, but I can provide an expanded prose interpretation:

The speaker examines what it means to be Arab through a mixture of personal memory, inherited wisdom, linguistic play, and grief. Childhood anecdotes and family stories initially make identity seem intimate and recognizable: it lives in relatives’ voices, familiar expressions, gestures, food, humor, and the sayings passed from one generation to another. These memories offer the speaker a sense of continuity, suggesting that Arabness is not merely a nationality or political category but a form of belonging rooted in family and culture.

At the same time, the speaker questions the traditional definitions used to identify a “true Arab.” Cultural sayings and wordplay expose how unstable such definitions can be. Language may preserve history and create community, but it can also reduce a complicated identity to clichés, inherited rules, or impossible standards. The speaker tests these ideas against lived experience and discovers that no proverb or clever turn of phrase can fully explain who belongs, what authenticity means, or how a people should respond to suffering.

This conflict becomes more painful as the speaker confronts news of Palestinian devastation. Images and reports of violence overwhelm the consolations of memory and the neatness of cultural definitions. Faced with death, displacement, and helplessness, language begins to fail. Familiar words sound inadequate, and even poetry seems incapable of containing the scale of grief. The speaker’s anguish comes partly from witnessing suffering at a distance and partly from recognizing it as inseparable from a shared history and identity.

Yet the collapse of language does not erase the need to speak. Instead, it reveals why belonging still matters. Arab identity emerges not as a test of purity but as an emotional and ethical bond—a commitment to remember, to grieve, and to recognize the humanity of others. Family memory and cultural inheritance cannot explain tragedy or repair it, but they give the speaker roots from which to respond.

Ultimately, the poem rejects rigid definitions of the “true Arab.” Identity survives less through slogans or qualifications than through compassion, solidarity, memory, and attachment to people and place. Although words cannot match the magnitude of Palestinian suffering, the attempt to speak remains an act of witness. In that tension—between language’s failure and the necessity of using it—the speaker finds a fragile but enduring sense of rootedness.
outputs.L5: An Arab traveler once said, “A true journey is not measured by distance, but by what it teaches the heart.” He crossed deserts and cities, meeting strangers who became friends. Along the way, he discovered that courage and kindness are strongest when shared—and that a true home can be found wherever people welcome one another.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person prose poem about an Arab American narrator remembering her father’s sayings while struggling to process devastating news from Palestine.
counterfactuals.output: My father measured grief in cups of coffee. *Drink,* he would say, pushing the small white cup toward me, *the heart needs something bitter it can finish.* This morning the news from Palestine keeps beginning again: another home opened to the sky, another mother calling a name into dust, another child learning how quickly the world can look away. I sit in my American kitchen with the refrigerator humming, the faucet obedient, the windows unbroken, and I do not know where to put my safety. My father used to say, *A wound does not ask for your passport.* He said, *The olive tree bends because it intends to remain.* He said, *When you cannot carry the whole country, carry one story.* So I carry his village as he gave it to me—stone terraces, figs split purple in the hand, the call to prayer threading dawn, his mother’s bread rising beneath a cloth. I carry the Palestine I inherited and the Palestine arriving now in unbearable images, and between them I feel my heart pulled like dough, stretched until light passes through. I want language large enough to shelter everyone. I want to reach through the screen and gather the dead back into their names. Instead, I whisper them when I can. I call my sister. I make coffee. Outside, the flag on the school hangs limp in the rain. Inside, my father’s voice moves through me: *Daughter, sorrow is also a homeland, but you must not build your only house there.* I press my palm to the table as if it were earth, as if beneath the wood there were roots, as if roots could cross oceans without permission. Then I drink what is bitter. Then I begin again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Condense a poem about inherited identity, the meaning of the name Shihab, childhood prejudice, and Palestinian suffering into one emotionally intense paragraph.
counterfactuals.output: My name is Shihab—a flame, a shooting star—an inheritance burning through generations, though as a child I learned how quickly others could twist it into something foreign, dangerous, less than human. Their taunts followed me home, where Palestine lived in stories, keys, olive trees, and wounds that never closed; and I understood that my name carried both light and grief, the sky’s brief brilliance and a people’s long suffering. Still, I hold it fiercely: proof that even beneath exile, prejudice, rubble, and mourning, we endure—we blaze, we fall, and we refuse to disappear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary monologue that begins with a father’s humorous definition of a “true Arab” and gradually turns into a meditation on headlines, displacement, language, and grief.
counterfactuals.output:
My father used to say a true Arab is a man who spends ten minutes insisting he is not hungry, then eats from everyone’s plate.

He would demonstrate this principle at dinner, shaking his head gravely while my mother set down the rice. No, no, he had eaten. He was full. He required nothing from this world. Then his hand would drift toward the lamb with the innocence of weather.

“A true Arab,” he continued, “never asks for directions. He consults the sun, insults the road, and arrives three hours late with a story.”

He had many definitions. A true Arab could repair any machine by striking it in the correct place. A true Arab believed tea was not a drink but a unit of time. A true Arab’s goodbye began at the door, continued on the stairs, crossed the street, and ended only when both parties had become small figures waving from opposite horizons.

As a child, I thought this was what belonging meant: the right to make fun of the habits that held you. Belonging was my father’s laughter, broad and theatrical, breaking over the table. It was my mother saying, Enough, you’ll teach the children nonsense. It was the blue bowl of olives, the bent teaspoon, the radio murmuring from the windowsill.

Then the radio learned to shout.

The names of cities began to arrive before breakfast. They came stripped of weather, stripped of weddings, stripped of the old men playing backgammon beneath striped awnings. A city that had once meant my aunt’s courtyard, apricots drying on a white sheet, became a number. Twelve dead. Forty wounded. Thousands displaced.

Displaced: a tidy word. It sounds almost polite, as if someone has moved a vase to dust the shelf.

No headline says: a woman has left behind the cup whose handle fit exactly between her fingers. No headline says: a boy keeps the key to a door now standing open to the sky. No headline records the basil plant abandoned on the balcony, leaning toward the sound of departure.

The newspapers preferred the passive voice. Homes were destroyed. Borders were closed. Shots were fired. People were killed. Events occurred without hands, without mouths giving orders, without anyone deciding that one life could be translated into a smaller word.

Casualty.

Migrant.

Refugee.

Body.

My father read those words at the kitchen table. He read them in the new country, under a pale northern light that made everything look unfinished. Outside, snow erased the pavement. Inside, he folded the paper along its hard black lines.

At first he made jokes.

“A true Arab,” he said, “can carry his entire homeland in two suitcases, provided his wife allows him six.”

My mother did not laugh. Or perhaps she did, once, softly, from another room.

In exile, language became a house with unreliable plumbing. My father spoke the new tongue carefully, as if crossing ice. He could ask for work, sign a form, explain where it hurt. But he could not be funny in it. His jokes arrived late or not at all. Their rhythm had been confiscated at the border.

He began to save Arabic for the telephone, for anger, for sleep.

Sometimes I heard him speaking to himself in the hallway. Not sentences—fragments. The names of trees. A proverb his mother used. The word for the smell of earth after rain. Words with no official purpose. Words that could not help him at the bank.

I answered him more and more in the language of school.

He would ask, in Arabic, Have you eaten?

I would say, Yeah.

He would ask, Are you cold?

I would say, I’m fine.

Between his questions and my answers, a country vanished.

Years later, when he began to forget, it was the new language that left him first. He misplaced its nouns, then its verbs. He stood in a supermarket holding an apple, unable to ask its price. Yet the old language returned bright and entire. He called me by my childhood name. He recited lines of poetry I had never learned. He asked when we were going home.

Which home? I wanted to ask.

The apartment above the bakery? The village now reachable only through photographs? The kitchen where the radio shouted? The graveyard we could not visit? Or this narrow house where the snow kept falling, where his coat hung by the door long after he no longer needed it?

But grief is another language in which I am not fluent.

After he died, I found his passports in a drawer, expired one after another, each containing a younger version of his face. In the oldest, he looked amused, as though the camera had interrupted him in the middle of a joke. In the last, he looked like a man waiting for a question no official knew how to ask.

I spread the documents across the table. Different seals. Different spellings of his name. Different governments attempting to define him.

None said: He loved figs.

None said: He sang badly while shaving.

None said: He could not pass a sleeping child without covering its feet.

The next morning, another city became a headline.

I read the article twice. I studied the map. I counted the dead because the dead had been given numbers, and numbers were the only part the paper promised not to forget.

Then I made tea the way my father had taught me: too strong, too sweet, enough for visitors who were not coming.

A true Arab, he once said, never drinks alone. He drinks with the living, the dead, and anyone who might knock.

So I set out two glasses.

I poured his first.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
